screens.title: Behavioral Patterns & the Strategy Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll enter the world of behavioral design patterns and focus on one of the most practical tools in a developer's toolbox: the Strategy pattern. Behavioral patterns are about how objects communicate and divide responsibilities so systems remain flexible and easier to maintain as requirements change. The Strategy pattern solves a common problem: an application needs to perform an operation with multiple possible algorithms, and we want to select or swap those algorithms without editing the client each time. You will see the core components — a strategy interface, concrete strategy implementations, and a context that delegates work — and a clear Java example that demonstrates swapping behaviors at runtime. We'll also walk through a small hands-on shipping-cost activity that mirrors real-world needs, and close with advice on when Strategy is useful and when it is overkill. By the end you'll be able to recognize where to replace brittle conditional logic with interchangeable algorithm objects and why that leads to code that follows the Open/Closed Principle. Consider this a practical blueprint for making behavior a first-class, replaceable concept in your designs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define the role of behavioral design patterns and explain why communication between objects matters. You will understand the core problem the Strategy pattern addresses: selecting among a family of algorithms without changing the client. You will implement the Strategy pattern in Java using a strategy interface, multiple concrete strategy classes, and a context that delegates behavior, and you will change strategies at runtime. You will also learn to identify scenarios that benefit from the Strategy pattern, for example replacing sprawling conditional logic in payment processing or shipping calculations. Finally, you will recognize common pitfalls such as over-engineering with strategies that never vary, or designing strategies that are too broad or too narrow. Each objective includes hands-on checkpoints so you can verify competency: implement a text formatter, implement at least two shipping strategies, and explain why the Open/Closed Principle is preserved. These objectives ensure you can both reason about when to apply Strategy and implement it in production code with minimal coupling.

screens.narratorSegment: These checkpoints translate objectives into concrete evidence. First, you should be able to write a strategy interface and at least two concrete strategies in Java that compile and run. Second, in a hands-on activity, implement a ShippingStrategy interface and two carrier strategies with the provided cost formulas; success means the ShoppingCart context computes different totals depending on the selected carrier. screens.title: What are Behavioral Design Patterns?
screens.narratorSegment: Behavioral design patterns describe how objects and classes interact to fulfill responsibilities. They are not primarily about object creation or structure; rather, they map the conversations and control flow between components. This matters because as systems grow, ad hoc message passing and interdependent logic create brittle code where small changes ripple across many classes. A behavioral pattern provides a tested blueprint: it identifies roles, messages, and delegation points so behavior can evolve with minimal impact. For example, if several components must decide how to perform a task, a behavioral pattern can centralize the decision or encapsulate varied behaviors into interchangeable objects. A common misconception is that behavioral patterns add unnecessary indirection. The right balance is that indirection is beneficial when behavior varies or needs to be extended; when behavior is stable and simple, indirection adds cost without value. Concretely, the Strategy pattern — which we focus on next — encapsulates a family of algorithms behind an interface so clients call a single method and can switch implementations without modification. Think of behavioral patterns as conversation rules that keep object interactions scalable and maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Behavioral patterns organize object interaction to make responsibilities clear and behavior easier to change without widespread edits.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Behavioral Patterns
What they do
Behavioral patterns specify how objects exchange responsibilities and control flow so behavior can change independently of callers.
  • • Define role-to-role communication between objects.
  • • Encapsulate algorithms or control policies as separate objects.
  • • Reduce coupling by delegating decisions to dedicated components.
  • Common misconception: unnecessary indirection when behavior never varies.
Concrete analogy
Imagine a restaurant kitchen where different chefs prepare the same dish with different recipes. The waiter requests a dish by name, not by how it is cooked. The recipes are interchangeable strategies; the waiter is the context delegating to a chosen chef.
Key Takeaway

Behavioral patterns make behavior a replaceable part of a system and keep callers stable while algorithms vary.

screens.title: The Strategy Pattern: Core Idea
screens.narratorSegment: At its core, the Strategy pattern provides a way to define a family of algorithms and make them interchangeable by encapsulating each algorithm behind a common interface. The context holds a reference to that interface and delegates algorithm execution to whatever concrete implementation has been provided. This separation has three practical effects: first, the context does not need to know the specifics of each algorithm, reducing coupling; second, new algorithms can be added without changing the context code, preserving the Open/Closed Principle; third, strategies can be chosen or swapped at runtime to respond to user preference or system configuration. A useful concrete example is a text formatter with implementations for plain, uppercase, and lowercase formatting. Instead of a conditional inside the editor selecting behavior, the editor simply asks the formatter to transform the text. A common misunderstanding is thinking Strategy is only for runtime selection. While runtime switching is a key advantage, Strategy also improves static design by separating concerns and making testing easier: each algorithm can be tested in isolation. Consider whether you have multiple related algorithms for one responsibility; if so, Strategy is an appropriate fit.

keyIdea.title: Strategy claim
keyIdea.text: Encapsulate related algorithms behind a simple interface so clients delegate behavior and algorithms can be added or swapped independently.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Strategy Pattern
Pattern structure
  • • Strategy Interface: declares the method clients use to run an algorithm.
  • • Concrete Strategies: implement the interface with specific algorithms.
  • • Context: holds a reference to a Strategy and delegates execution.
When to use: multiple algorithms for the same task, need to swap behaviors at runtime, or to remove large conditional blocks that select behavior.
Mini example
Think of a text formatter interface with three implementations: plain, uppercase, and lowercase. The editor delegates formatting to the strategy rather than switching on a type code. Add a new formatter, like reverse text, by creating another strategy class without touching the editor.
Key Takeaway

Strategy decouples the 'what' from the 'how'—clients request work and strategies provide implementations.

screens.title: Strategy Pattern Components
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the three components of Strategy makes implementation straightforward. The Strategy interface declares the method signature used to run algorithms; it is intentionally small and focused. Concrete strategy classes implement that interface, each encapsulating one algorithm. They should be cohesive: each class represents a single, well-defined way of performing the task. The Context holds a reference to the Strategy interface and delegates execution by calling the interface method. The Context should not depend on concrete strategy implementations; it only needs the interface. This design allows you to inject different strategies at creation or change them at runtime through a setter. A typical mistake is giving the strategy interface too many responsibilities — add only the methods required for the algorithms. Another mistake is making strategies too fine-grained; dozens of tiny classes with near-identical behavior increase maintenance cost. In practice, pick a strategy boundary that captures the meaningful variation in behavior, and keep the interface minimal so Context remains simple and testable. Strategy Pattern Components means strategy = (interface) + (concrete implementations) + (context delegator); keep interfaces narrow and strategies cohesive.. In practical terms, interface, concrete strategies, and context explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Components
Strategy Interface
Declare the single method clients call. Keep it minimal to avoid overburdening implementers.
Concrete Strategies
Each class implements the interface with a specific algorithm. They should be cohesive and testable in isolation.
Context
Holds a reference to the Strategy interface and delegates execution. It should not know concrete types.
Pro Tip
Inject strategies via constructor for immutability, and provide a setter when runtime switching is required.
Common Mistake
Make sure your interface isn't a grab-bag of unrelated methods; that signals poor separation of concerns.
Check Your Understanding
If adding a new algorithm requires editing Context, Strategy is not applied correctly. Why?

screens.title: TextFormatter Example: Interface and Implementations
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look at the TextFormatter example to ground the pattern in runnable code. The strategy interface declares a single method, format, which accepts a string and returns the transformed text. The example provides three concrete strategies: PlainTextFormatter returns the input unchanged, UpperCaseFormatter converts the string to uppercase, and LowerCaseFormatter converts it to lowercase. This simple interface and focused implementations make each formatter easy to unit test and extend. A common misconception is that Strategy requires complex APIs; in practice a single, well-named method is often enough. When you add a new formatter, such as a ReverseTextFormatter, you create a new class implementing the interface and plug it into the TextEditor context without editing the editor itself. The benefit is immediate: clear separation of concerns, small classes focused on one algorithm, and the ability to swap behavior at runtime or via dependency injection. Keep strategy classes small and descriptive so their intent is obvious. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › TextFormatter Example
Strategy Interface (visual)
public interface TextFormatter {
    String format(String text);
}
Concrete Strategies (visual)
public class PlainTextFormatter implements TextFormatter {
    @Override
    public String format(String text) { return text; }
}

public class UpperCaseFormatter implements TextFormatter {
    @Override
    public String format(String text) { return text.toUpperCase(); }
}

public class LowerCaseFormatter implements TextFormatter {
    @Override
    public String format(String text) { return text.toLowerCase(); }
}
Concrete example
Use PlainTextFormatter for raw output, UpperCaseFormatter for emphasis, and LowerCaseFormatter when normalizing input for comparisons. Each strategy is a single responsibility.
Key Takeaway

Small, focused strategy classes keep algorithms isolated and swapable without changing clients.

screens.title: TextEditor Context: Delegation and Runtime Switching
screens.narratorSegment: The TextEditor class demonstrates the Context role in the Strategy pattern. It stores a reference to a TextFormatter and calls its format method when publishing text. Crucially, it provides a setter to replace the current formatter at runtime. This approach eliminates conditional branching inside the editor and moves variation into strategy classes. In practice you might inject the initial formatter via the constructor, then allow switching with a setFormatter method when the user changes preferences. Running the example produces three outputs as you swap formatters: the original text, uppercase, then lowercase. One subtle point: the Context should avoid depending on concrete strategy behavior; it should treat the result as the formatted string without inspecting how it was produced. A common mistake is to let the context assume too much about the returned value or to fetch implementation-specific details from strategies. Keep the contract simple: request work, accept the result, and don't peek inside the strategy. TextEditor Context: Delegation and Runtime Switching means context delegates to a strategy and can swap strategies at runtime; keep the contract simple and avoid assumptions about concrete implementations.. In practical terms, the context holds a strategy and delegates formatting requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

TextEditor (visual)
public class TextEditor {
    private TextFormatter formatter;

    public TextEditor(TextFormatter formatter) { this.formatter = formatter; }

    public void setFormatter(TextFormatter formatter) { this.formatter = formatter; }

screens.title: Switch Statement vs Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Many codebases start by choosing an algorithm using conditional statements: if-else chains or switch blocks based on a type code. This approach centralizes decision logic and quickly becomes hard to maintain as new options are added. The Strategy pattern moves selection out of the client. Instead of branching, the client receives a strategy object that already encapsulates the chosen algorithm. The process is straightforward: identify the varying behavior, extract an interface declaring the operation, implement concrete strategies for each branch, and replace the conditional with a strategy lookup and injection. This reduces the number of places you need to edit when adding new behavior and keeps each algorithm isolated. A misconception is that Strategy only helps runtime selection; it also improves static structure and testability. A concrete scenario: a report generator with many formats—Strategy lets you add a new formatter class rather than adding another branch to the generator's method. The final result is cleaner code, easier tests, and adherence to the Open/Closed Principle. Switch Statement vs Strategy means extract the varying behavior into strategies to replace conditional logic with polymorphic delegation and improve maintainability.. In practical terms, how strategy replaces conditional selection with polymorphism. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Switch vs Strategy
If-else / switch approach
Centralized branching: add another branch for each new algorithm. Problems: violates Open/Closed Principle and hurts readability.
Example smell: a long method where each branch contains distinct algorithmic logic and the method grows with new requirements.
Strategy approach
Extract an interface and move each branch into a concrete strategy class. The client delegates to the strategy instead of branching.
Key Takeaway

Strategy replaces branching with polymorphism, improving extensibility and testability.

screens.narratorSegment: The chapter's hands-on activity asks you to implement shipping cost strategies for an e-commerce application. Start by defining a ShippingStrategy interface with a method that accepts weight and distance and returns a cost. A practical test is to run checkout with identical inputs and observe different totals for FedEx and UPS. This activity mirrors real systems where carriers change pricing rules independently of the cart implementation. keyIdea.title: Checkout flow
keyIdea.text: ShoppingCart delegates shipping calculations to the active strategy, enabling different totals without modifying checkout logic.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › ShoppingCart Context
ShoppingCart (visual)
public class ShoppingCart {
    private ShippingStrategy shippingStrategy;

    public ShoppingCart(ShippingStrategy strategy) { this.shippingStrategy = strategy; }

    public void setShippingStrategy(ShippingStrategy strategy) { this.shippingStrategy = strategy; }

    public double checkout(double totalWeight, double totalDistance) {
        double productCost = 100.0; // assumed
        double shippingCost = shippingStrategy.calculateCost(totalWeight, totalDistance);
        System.out.println("Calculating shipping cost for weight " + totalWeight + " kg and distance " + totalDistance + " km.");
        System.out.println("Shipping cost using " + shippingStrategy.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": $" + String.format("%.2f", shippingCost));
        return productCost + shippingCost;
    }
}
Practical exercise: instantiate the cart with FedEx, run checkout, then set UPS and run checkout again to see differing totals for the same inputs.

screens.title: Benefits vs Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Strategy brings several architectural benefits: it reduces conditional complexity, enables runtime selection, supports the Open/Closed Principle by allowing new algorithms to be added without editing clients, and improves testability since each strategy can be tested in isolation. However, applying Strategy indiscriminately creates costs. If an algorithm is simple, stable, and unlikely to have alternatives, extracting a strategy adds indirection and more classes to maintain. Another pitfall is poor granularity: strategies that are too broad mix concerns, while strategies that are too fine-grained lead to class explosion. A good rule of thumb is to apply Strategy when you actually have or expect multiple, distinct algorithms for the same responsibility. Also avoid exposing implementation details through the strategy interface. Keep interfaces narrow and document the expected contract. Finally, consider whether simpler techniques, such as passing a function or using a configuration flag, would suffice for small variations before introducing Strategy. screens.title: Anti-patterns and Misuse
screens.narratorSegment: When applying Strategy be mindful of common anti-patterns. One is extracting Strategy too early for behavior that will never vary; this creates extra classes and indirection for no gain. Another is making the strategy interface an anemic bag of unrelated methods, forcing implementations to implement functionality they don't need. A related error is letting the Context inspect or downcast a strategy to access implementation-specific behavior, which reintroduces coupling. Avoid proliferation of minute strategies that only differ by a constant; prefer parameterized strategies in those cases. Also watch for duplication: if several strategies share substantial code, consider refactoring shared behavior into a base class or a helper component. Finally, ensure your testing strategy includes unit tests for each strategy and integration tests that verify the context with different strategies. These practices will help you use Strategy to increase clarity rather than scattering responsibility across many tiny, hard-to-manage classes. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll enter the world of behavioral design patterns and focus on one of the most practical tools in a developer's toolbox: the Strategy pattern. Behavioral patterns are about how objects communicate and divide responsibilities so systems remain flexible and easier to maintain as requirements change. The Strategy pattern solves a common problem: an application needs to perform an operation with multiple possible algorithms, and we want to select or swap those algorithms without editing the client each time. You will see the core components — a strategy interface, concrete strategy implementations, and a context that delegates work — and a clear Java example that demonstrates swapping behaviors at runtime. We'll also walk through a small hands-on shipping-cost activity that mirrors real-world needs, and close with advice on when Strategy is useful and when it is overkill. By the end you'll be able to recognize where to replace brittle conditional logic with interchangeable algorithm objects and why that leads to code that follows the Open/Closed Principle. Consider this a practical blueprint for making behavior a first-class, replaceable concept in your designs.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define the role of behavioral design patterns and explain why communication between objects matters. You will understand the core problem the Strategy pattern addresses: selecting among a family of algorithms without changing the client. You will implement the Strategy pattern in Java using a strategy interface, multiple concrete strategy classes, and a context that delegates behavior, and you will change strategies at runtime. You will also learn to identify scenarios that benefit from the Strategy pattern, for example replacing sprawling conditional logic in payment processing or shipping calculations. Finally, you will recognize common pitfalls such as over-engineering with strategies that never vary, or designing strategies that are too broad or too narrow. Each objective includes hands-on checkpoints so you can verify competency: implement a text formatter, implement at least two shipping strategies, and explain why the Open/Closed Principle is preserved. These objectives ensure you can both reason about when to apply Strategy and implement it in production code with minimal coupling.

These checkpoints translate objectives into concrete evidence. First, you should be able to write a strategy interface and at least two concrete strategies in Java that compile and run. For the TextEditor example, success means producing the three outputs shown: plain, uppercase, and lowercase formatted text, then swapping strategies at runtime to produce different outputs without modifying the TextEditor. Second, in a hands-on activity, implement a ShippingStrategy interface and two carrier strategies with the provided cost formulas; success means the ShoppingCart context computes different totals depending on the selected carrier. Third, you should be able to explain why this approach follows the Open/Closed Principle: new strategies extend behavior without changing existing context code. Finally, you should be able to identify a misuse: introducing Strategy for a single, stable algorithm adds unnecessary complexity. These checkpoints keep the lesson practical: build runnable examples, reason about design, and avoid over-engineering when a simple function would do.

Behavioral design patterns describe how objects and classes interact to fulfill responsibilities. They are not primarily about object creation or structure; rather, they map the conversations and control flow between components. This matters because as systems grow, ad hoc message passing and interdependent logic create brittle code where small changes ripple across many classes. A behavioral pattern provides a tested blueprint: it identifies roles, messages, and delegation points so behavior can evolve with minimal impact. For example, if several components must decide how to perform a task, a behavioral pattern can centralize the decision or encapsulate varied behaviors into interchangeable objects. A common misconception is that behavioral patterns add unnecessary indirection. The right balance is that indirection is beneficial when behavior varies or needs to be extended; when behavior is stable and simple, indirection adds cost without value. Concretely, the Strategy pattern — which we focus on next — encapsulates a family of algorithms behind an interface so clients call a single method and can switch implementations without modification. Think of behavioral patterns as conversation rules that keep object interactions scalable and maintainable.

At its core, the Strategy pattern provides a way to define a family of algorithms and make them interchangeable by encapsulating each algorithm behind a common interface. The context holds a reference to that interface and delegates algorithm execution to whatever concrete implementation has been provided. This separation has three practical effects: first, the context does not need to know the specifics of each algorithm, reducing coupling; second, new algorithms can be added without changing the context code, preserving the Open/Closed Principle; third, strategies can be chosen or swapped at runtime to respond to user preference or system configuration. A useful concrete example is a text formatter with implementations for plain, uppercase, and lowercase formatting. Instead of a conditional inside the editor selecting behavior, the editor simply asks the formatter to transform the text. A common misunderstanding is thinking Strategy is only for runtime selection. While runtime switching is a key advantage, Strategy also improves static design by separating concerns and making testing easier: each algorithm can be tested in isolation. Consider whether you have multiple related algorithms for one responsibility; if so, Strategy is an appropriate fit.

Understanding the three components of Strategy makes implementation straightforward. The Strategy interface declares the method signature used to run algorithms; it is intentionally small and focused. Concrete strategy classes implement that interface, each encapsulating one algorithm. They should be cohesive: each class represents a single, well-defined way of performing the task. The Context holds a reference to the Strategy interface and delegates execution by calling the interface method. The Context should not depend on concrete strategy implementations; it only needs the interface. This design allows you to inject different strategies at creation or change them at runtime through a setter. A typical mistake is giving the strategy interface too many responsibilities — add only the methods required for the algorithms. Another mistake is making strategies too fine-grained; dozens of tiny classes with near-identical behavior increase maintenance cost. In practice, pick a strategy boundary that captures the meaningful variation in behavior, and keep the interface minimal so Context remains simple and testable. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's look at the TextFormatter example to ground the pattern in runnable code. The strategy interface declares a single method, format, which accepts a string and returns the transformed text. The example provides three concrete strategies: PlainTextFormatter returns the input unchanged, UpperCaseFormatter converts the string to uppercase, and LowerCaseFormatter converts it to lowercase. This simple interface and focused implementations make each formatter easy to unit test and extend.
